title: A friend gives the hard thing
word: A friend gives the hard thing
hook: seven marks of a friend: gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, bears what is hard to bear
carry: a friend gives the hard thing

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old Buddha in the sun, and your line, even his. Did your body or someone else's ask for care? Yesterday's scene was also a friendship: Ananda's hands on his teacher's arms. Today, what makes a friend. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Think about who you'd call at three in the morning. Not the people who like your posts. The ones who'd pick up. Most of us could name them on one hand, and the list doesn't always match the people we see the most. The Book of Sevens has a short sutta that tries to put that list into words. It's addressed to the monks, but there's nothing monastic about it. It's seven marks of someone worth being friends with, someone you should keep close even if they push you away. Today: a friend gives the hard thing.
screen: `WHO WOULD PICK UP AT 3AM?` → `NOT ALWAYS WHO WE SEE MOST.` → `SEVEN MARKS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: A friend with seven qualities, the Buddha says, is worth associating with. One: they give what is hard to give. Two: they do what is hard to do. Three: they bear what is hard to bear. Four: they tell you their secrets. Five: they keep your secrets. Six: they don't abandon you in misfortune. Seven: they don't look down on you when you're ruined. Notice the first three. Hard to give, hard to do, hard to bear. Anyone can give what's easy: a like, a quick text, the thing they didn't need anyway. A friend is the one who gives what costs something. Their Saturday. Their honesty, when it's awkward. The patience to sit through your bad month. Then four and five, a pair: trust going both ways. They let you in, and they don't let your life out. And six and seven: the friend who stays when things fall apart, and who doesn't treat you differently when you've lost. That last one is sharp. People often visit success. Fewer visit ruin. The sutta ends in verse, and the verse adds a line worth remembering: such a friend should be kept close, even if they'd turn you away. Two days ago, the six ways to be dear described what makes a community hold. This is the same thing at the size of two people. And the sutta can be read both ways at once: a list of friends to look for, and a list of how to be one.
screen: `HARD TO GIVE, DO, BEAR.` · `SECRETS SHARED, SECRETS KEPT.` · `STAYS IN MISFORTUNE.` · then, large: `A FRIEND GIVES THE HARD THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be one of the seven. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind a friend who once gave you something hard: time, honesty, patience, presence when things were bad. Let yourself feel grateful for a few breaths. Then turn it around. Bring to mind a friend who might need something hard from you right now. Which of the seven could you be for them this week? Give the hard thing, bear the hard thing, keep the secret, stay. Choose one. The bell holds the time.
A friend gives the hard thing. From the Book of Sevens: a true friend gives, does and bears what's hard, shares and keeps secrets, and stays through misfortune and ruin. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: a friend gives the hard thing. Today, give one friend something that costs you a little: time, attention, an honest word. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often pair this sutta with the Buddha's teaching on good friendship, kalyanamittata, and many lay Buddhists read it as advice both for choosing friends and for being one.

fork.setup: you have two friends. one sends a quick text every day. one shows up once, on the worst night of your year. by the sutta's marks, which is the friend?
options: the one who showed up when it was hard.
fork.reveal: the sutta's friend gives what's hard to give and doesn't abandon you in misfortune. it's not about how often, but about what it costs.

original.note: Pali mitta: friend; the root of metta, loving-kindness, the friend's feeling.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good friend is someone who's always nice.
what it means: AN 7.36 says a friend gives, does and bears what's hard, and stays through ruin.
what a scholar hears: a nearly matching list of a true friend's marks appears in the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha's advice to a young householder.

notes: AN 7.36 paraphrased. Confirm the seven qualities in order and the verse line about keeping the friend close 'even if turned away'.

Trapdoor: DN 31's lists of true friends are related but not identical; 'nearly matching' may be overstated. Confirm or soften.
'People often visit success. Fewer visit ruin' is the writer's line, not the text's.
